text:
How can we find \hat{\bm{\theta}}?













Exercise 3.1 (Gradient descent on a quadratic) Derive a closed-form trajectory for gradient descent on F(\bm{\theta}) = \frac{1}{2} \|\mathbf{A}\bm{\theta} - \mathbf{b}\|^2 initialised at \bm{\theta}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^p.
Deduce an upper bound on the learning rate \epsilon > 0, below which convergence to a global minimum is guaranteed.

Solution
The gradient is \nabla F(\bm{\theta}) = \mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{A} \bm{\theta} - \mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{b}, so gradient descent satisfies \bm{\theta}_t = \bm{\theta}_{t-1} - \epsilon (\mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{A} \bm{\theta}_{t-1} - \mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{b}). In particular, if \bm{\theta}_\star is any minimiser of F then \mathbf{A}\bm{\theta}_\star = \mathbf{b} and we can re-write the gradient descent update as \bm{\theta}_t - \bm{\theta}_\star = (\mathbf{I} - \epsilon \mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{A})(\bm{\theta}_{t-1} - \bm{\theta}_\star). Unwinding the recursion, 
\bm{\theta}_t - \bm{\theta}_\star = (\mathbf{I} - \epsilon \mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{A})^t(\bm{\theta}_0 - \bm{\theta}_\star) .
 To reason about the size of the right hand side we can consider the eigenvalues of \mathbf{I} - \epsilon \mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{A}. Let \lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{M}) and \lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{M}) indicate the smallest and largest eigenvalues of a matrix \mathbf{M}. Assume \mathbf{A} \neq \mathbf{0} else \bm{\theta}_0 is already a minimiser of F. Then \lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{A}) > 0. For \epsilon < 1 / \lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{A}) we have 
\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{I} - \epsilon \mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{A}) < 1 - \epsilon \lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{A}) < 1 - \frac{ \lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{A}) }{ \lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{A}) } < 1
 and thus 
\| \bm{\theta}_t - \bm{\theta}_\star \|
\leq \left( 1 - \frac{ \lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{A}) }{ \lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{A}) } \right)^t \| \bm{\theta}_0 - \bm{\theta}_\star \| \rightarrow 0
 as t \rightarrow \infty, showing that gradient descent is convergent1.














Definition 3.1 (Convex function) A differentiable function F : \mathbb{R}^p \rightarrow \mathbb{R} is convex if 
F(\bm{\vartheta}) \geq F(\bm{\theta}) + \nabla F(\bm{\theta})^\top (\bm{\vartheta} - \bm{\theta})
 for all \bm{\theta}, \bm{\vartheta} \in \mathbb{R}^d.









\begin{algorithm} \caption{Gradient Descent on $F : \mathbb{R}^p \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$} \begin{algorithmic} \Require gradients $\nabla F : \mathbb{R}^p \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^p$ \Require initial state $\bm{\theta}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^p$ \Require learning rate $\epsilon \in (0,\infty)$ \Require number of steps $T$ \Ensure final parameter estimate $\bm{\theta}_T$ \For{$t = 0, \dots, T-1$} \State $\bm{\theta}_{t+1} \gets \bm{\theta}_t - \epsilon \nabla F(\bm{\theta}_t)$ \EndFor \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}









Theorem 3.1 (Convergence of gradient descent) Let F : \mathbb{R}^p \rightarrow \mathbb{R} be convex and differentiable with \|\nabla F(\bm{\theta})\| \leq B for all \bm{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^p. Then the sequence (\bm{\theta}_t)_{t \geq 0} produced by gradient descent as in Algorithm 1 satisfies 
\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1} F(\bm{\theta}_t) - F(\bm{\theta}_\star) \leq  \frac{\|\bm{\theta}_0 - \bm{\theta}_\star\|^2}{2\epsilon T}  + \frac{\epsilon B^2}{2}
\tag{3.3} where \bm{\theta}_\star denotes any minimiser of F.












NoteProof






Proof 3.1. From the definition of gradient descent

\begin{align*}
\|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1} - \boldsymbol{\theta}_\star\|^2 & = \|\boldsymbol{\theta}_t - \epsilon \nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t) - \boldsymbol{\theta}_\star\|^2 \\[0.5em]
& = \|\boldsymbol{\theta}_t - \boldsymbol{\theta}_\star\|^2 - 2 \epsilon \nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)^\top (\boldsymbol{\theta}_t - \boldsymbol{\theta}_\star) + \epsilon^2 \underbrace{ \|\nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)\|^2 }_{\leq B^2}
\end{align*}
 and thus 
\nabla F(\bm{\theta}_t)^\top (\bm{\theta}_t - \bm{\theta}_\star)  \leq \frac{1}{2\epsilon} \left\{ \|\bm{\theta}_t - \bm{\theta}_\star\|^2 - \|\bm{\theta}_{t+1} - \bm{\theta}_\star\|^2 \right\} + \frac{1}{2} \epsilon B^2 .
\tag{3.5} Now, since F is convex 3.1 we know that 
    F(\bm{\theta}_t) - F(\bm{\theta}_\star)  \leq \nabla F(\bm{\theta}_t)^\top (\bm{\theta}_t - \bm{\theta}_\star) .
\tag{3.6} Using Equation 3.5 to bound the right hand side of Equation 3.6 leads to 
\begin{align*}
    F(\bm{\theta}_t)  - F(\bm{\theta}_\star)   & \leq \frac{1}{2 \epsilon} \left\{ \|\bm{\theta}_t - \bm{\theta}_\star\|^2 - \|\bm{\theta}_{t+1} - \bm{\theta}_\star\|^2 \right\} + \frac{1}{2} \epsilon B^2 .
\end{align*}
 Averaging both sides over t, and noting the telescopic sum (\sum_{t=0}^{T-1} x_{t+1} - x_t = x_T - x_0), 
\begin{align*}
    \frac{1}{T}  \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} F(\bm{\theta}_t) - F(\bm{\theta}_\star) & \leq \frac{1}{2\epsilon T} \left\{ \|\bm{\theta}_0 - \bm{\theta}_\star\|^2 - \underbrace{ \|\bm{\theta}_T - \bm{\theta}_\star\|^2 }_{\geq 0} \right\} + \frac{1}{2} \epsilon B^2  \\
    & \leq \frac{\|\bm{\theta}_0 - \bm{\theta}_\star\|^2}{2\epsilon T}  + \frac{\epsilon B^2}{2} ,
\end{align*}
 completing the argument.

title: 3  Stochastic Optimisation
3  Stochastic Optimisation
text:
3.3 Beyond “Vanilla” Stochastic Gradient Descent 
Stochastic gradient descent is a popular and effective optimisation method for training machine learning models, but it can be quite slow in general.
Several ideas have emerged that aim to accelerate convergence in stochastic optimisation; in fact we have already seen a simple example, in the form of a time-dependent learning rate \epsilon_t in Section 3.1.
Here we briefly discuss some of the other extensions that are most commonly used.

Momentum is an enhancement to stochastic gradient descent that helps accelerate convergence by “smoothing out” the fluctuations in the stochastic gradient.
The gradient update with momentum looks like 
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\rho}_{t+1} &= \beta \boldsymbol{\rho}_t + (1 - \beta)\,\nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t), \\
\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1} &= \boldsymbol{\theta}_t - \epsilon \boldsymbol{\rho}_{t+1}.
\end{aligned}
 where \beta is the momentum coefficient.
By adding a proportion \beta of the previous direction \boldsymbol{\rho}_t to the current direction \boldsymbol{\rho}_{t+1}, momentum helps the optimiser move in a consistent direction, reducing oscillations (as illustrated in the right panel of Figure 3.2) and often speeding up convergence as a result.
Adaptive learning rates allow for the learning rate \epsilon_t to be increased or decreased based on observed gradients \nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t), \nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1}), \dots. The idea is useful because manual selection of \epsilon is often a difficult task (e.g. because B in Theorem 3.2 will be unknown in general). The intuition for adapting the learning rate is that if the gradients are large then a small step size should typically be used, and conversely if the gradients are small then a large step size should typically be used. A famous example is Adagrad: 
\epsilon_t
=
\frac{\epsilon_0}{
  \sqrt{\sum_{s \le t} \lVert \nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_s) \rVert^2} + \zeta
} ,
 where \zeta > 0 is some small constant to avoid division by 0.
Gradient clipping can be useful in settings where occasionally a very large value of the gradient \nabla F is encountered. This can occur when dealing with a complex loss landscape, where some areas of the parameter space give rise to a very steep gradient (e.g. as illustrated in the right part of Figure 2.10). The idea is simply to replace the “raw” gradients \nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta}) with a clipped version, such as 
\begin{cases}
\nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta}),
& \text{if } \lVert \nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \rVert < \tau, \\[4pt]
\dfrac{\tau}{\lVert \nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \rVert}
\nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta}),
& \text{if } \lVert \nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \rVert \ge \tau,
\end{cases}
 where \tau controls the largest allowed norm of a gradient.

Each of these improvements aims to address specific limitations of the basic stochastic gradient descent algorithm, such as slow convergence, sensitivity to tuning parameters, and difficulty in navigating complex loss landscapes.
By carefully selecting and combining these techniques, it is often possible to significantly enhance the performance and efficiency of stochastic optimisation when training a machine learning model.






TipRemark (Learning to learn)






Remark 3.1 (Learning to learn). It is common to view the search for a good optimiser as a supervised machine learning task in its own right, and to describe this concept the phrase learning to learn is sometimes used.










TipRemark (Gradient descent as a biological analogy for learning in neural networks?)






Remark 3.2 (Gradient descent as a biological analogy for learning in neural networks?). The biological interpretation of neural networks as a model of the brain is generally considered sound, but attempts to interpret training via (stochastic) gradient descent as an analogue of how the brain learns in the real world is controversial (Lillicrap et al. 2020).

title: 3  Stochastic Optimisation
text:
3.4 Automatic Differentiation 
It is remarkable that complex machine learning models can now be defined and trained using just a few lines of code in a high-level programming language like PyTorch. The key engineering breakthrough that makes all of this possible is automatic differentiation; the ability to quickly compute gradients such as \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{R}_n(f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}). Though differentiation is in no way a novel concept, what separates automatic differentiation from alternatives such as “numerical differentiation” based on finite–difference formulae, for example 
f'(x) \approx \frac{ f(x + \delta) - f(x - \delta) }{2 \delta},
 is that automatic differentiation is exact (at least, in exact arithmetic) while oftentimes also being fast.







Example 3.1 (Automatic differentiation from scratch) For the sake of illustration, suppose we wish to build an automatic differentiation tool from scratch. The first step would be to define the elementary functions in a way that also encodes instructions for how these elementary functions are differentiated. Taking the sine function as an example:
import math

def sin_ad(x, dx=1.0):
    f = math.sin(x)
    df = math.cos(x) * dx
    return f, df
Here, sin_ad returns both the usual function value \sin(x), and the analytic derivative \cos(x). A rich framework like PyTorch will include essentially all of the elementary functions we can think of, with names such as torch.sin; we simply illustrate the idea here by adding one more function to our toolkit, the exponential:
def exp_ad(x, dx=1.0):
    f = math.exp(x)
    df = math.exp(x) * dx
    return f, df
Armed with at least some of the elementary functions, we can now try to compute the derivative of composite functions such as 
f(x) = \exp(\sin(x)) , \qquad x = \frac{\pi}{4} .
 To do so we will first compute y = \sin(x) and then \exp(y) in what is called forward mode differentiation:
x = math.pi / 4   # input
dx = 1.0          # derivative of x w.r.t itself
y, dy = sin_ad(x, dx)
f, df = exp_ad(y, dy)
The output f is the function value f(x), while df represents the derivative f'(x) of interest. Tracking back through the computation, we can see that forward mode differentiation is an explicit implementation of the chain rule 
f'(x) = \exp'(\sin(x)) \sin'(x) = \exp(\sin(x)) \cos(x)
 which of course in this small example we could have implemented by hand.




This example is shown only for illustrative purposes; where frameworks such as PyTorch or JAX excel is in performing fast vectorised computations in a memory-efficient way, often on one or more GPUs. Automatic differentiation has revolutionised machine learning and underpins the recent AI boom; we argue that the contributors to these tools deserve greater credit.






TipRemark (Forward versus backward)






Remark 3.3 (Forward versus backward). Example 3.1 demonstrated so-called forward mode differentiation, where derivatives are computed in the direction from input to output. This is generally more efficient when dealing with functions with many outputs and few inputs.
Reverse mode is often preferred for functions with many inputs and few outputs, such as most neural networks, as it computes the derivatives in the reverse order, allowing gradients to be calculated more efficiently.








Bach, Francis. 2024. Learning Theory from First Principles. MIT Press.


Lillicrap, Timothy P, Adam Santoro, Luke Marris, Colin J Akerman, and Geoffrey Hinton. 2020. “Backpropagation and the Brain.” Nature Reviews Neuroscience 21 (6): 335–46.

The quantity \lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{M}) / \lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{M}) is called the reciprocal condition number of the matrix \mathbf{M}; this is always between 0 and 1, and is closer to 0 when \mathbf{M} has an “effective low rank”.↩︎
The random subset is refreshed at each step of the gradient descent, so eventually and with high probability all of the data are used, just not all at the same time.↩︎

title: 4  Generalisation Error
text:
4.1 Generalisation Error Bounds
Statistical learning theory broadly refers to the mathematical analysis of generalisation error, which captures how close our machine learning models are to being optimal:
Generalisation error occurs because in practice we only have access to a finite training dataset, meaning that the true (or “real world”) risk functional \mathcal{R}(\cdot) cannot be exactly minimised. The generalisation error will depend on both the choice of machine learning model and how it is trained. Since f_n \in \mathcal{F} it is clear that the generalisation error is non-negative in general.
Statistical learning theory is a deep topic, and we will content ourselves in this module to see only the most basic analytic result, on the generalisation error of empirical risk minimisation, together with some of the key terminology.
For this we need to be familiar with Hoeffding’s concentration inequality:
To enable a simple theoretical argument, in the following we restrict attention to the case where the machine learning model is a finite set \mathcal{F}. This is admittedly a bit artificial, but this setting does occur in practice, e.g. when there already exist multiple pretrained machine learning models for a given task, and from these we need to select a single “best” pre-trained model (e.g. selecting a “best” large language model for a natural language processing task).
Theorem 4.1 captures some of the basic intuition that we would expect; as the number training data n \rightarrow \infty, the generalisation error converges to 0. Further, the size of the generalisation error is controlled by the size of the machine learning model \mathcal{F}, and if we require a higher probability bound (i.e. smaller \delta) then we must accept a looser bound on the generalisation error.
A nice aspect of Theorem 4.1 is that it does not place any restriction on the data-generating distribution P or the loss function L that define the statistical task (with the exception that L is assumed to take values in [0,1], but this is just to enable a straightforward application of Hoeffding’s inequality and is not a fundamental limitation of this type of result).
Generalisation error bounds are useful because they tell us how much data are required to achieve a nominal performance level:
There is a rich mathematical theory dealing with the case where L can be unbounded and \mathcal{F} can be infinite, involving interesting and deep mathematical concepts such as empirical process theory, Rademacher complexity, and VC-dimension. A good reference is Bach (2024, chap. 4).

title: 4  Generalisation Error
text:
Proposition 4.1 (Hoeffding’s Inequality) Let Z_1 , \dots , Z_n be independent and identically distributed random variables with mean \mu, and taking values in [0,1]. Then, for any t > 0, 
\mathbb{P}\left( \left| \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i - \mu  \right| \geq t \right) \leq 2 \exp( - 2 n t^2  ) .













Theorem 4.1 (Generalisation error for empirical risk minimisation) Consider the setting of Definition 1.1 and let |\mathcal{F}| < \infty, n \in \mathbb{N}, and \delta \in (0,1) be fixed. Let the loss function L take values in [0,1]. Then, with probability at least 1 - \delta, 
\mathcal{R}(f_n) - \min_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(f) \leq \sqrt{ \frac{2}{n} \log \frac{2 |\mathcal{F}| }{\delta} } .












NoteProof (Theorem 4.1)






Proof 4.1 (Theorem 4.1). For each f \in \mathcal{F} we have from Hoeffding’s inequality 4.1 that, for any t > 0, 
\mathbb{P}\left( \underbrace{ | \mathcal{R}_n(f) - \mathcal{R}(f)  | \geq t }_{= A_f} \right) \leq 2 \exp( - 2 n t^2  ) .
 Now, we wish to bound the probability that the events A_f hold simultaneously for all f, and since \mathcal{F} is a finite set, we can do this via a union bound: 
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}\left( \cup_{f \in \mathcal{F}} A_f \right) & \leq \sum_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathbb{P}(A_f) \\
& \leq \sum_{f \in \mathcal{F}} 2 \exp( - 2 n t^2  )
= 2 |\mathcal{F}|  \exp( - 2 n t^2  ) .
\end{align*}
 Thus, with probability at least 1 - 2 |\mathcal{F}|  \exp( - 2 n t^2  ) we have that | \mathcal{R}_n(f) - \mathcal{R}(f)  | < t simultaneously for all f \in \mathcal{F}. This shows that, with high probability, we have uniform convergence of \mathcal{R}_n(\cdot) to \mathcal{R}(\cdot). To polish the presentation, take \delta =  2 |\mathcal{F}|  \exp( - 2 n t^2  ) so that 
t = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{2n} \log \left( \frac{2|\mathcal{F}|}{\delta} \right) } .
 Finally, letting f_\star \in \argmin_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(f) minimise the (population) risk \mathcal{R}(\cdot), and recalling that the empirical risk is denoted \mathcal{R}_n(\cdot) (cf. Definition 1.4), we have that with probability at least 1 - \delta, 
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{R}(f_n) & \leq \mathcal{R}_n(f_n) + t \qquad \text{(uniform convergence)} \\
& \leq \mathcal{R}_n(f_\star)  + t \qquad \text{(since $f_n$ is a minimiser of $\mathcal{R}_n$)} \\
& \leq \mathcal{R}(f_\star)  + 2 t  \qquad \text{(uniform convergence)}
\end{align*}
 completing the argument.












TipRemark (Sample Complexity)






Remark 4.1 (Sample Complexity). In the context of Theorem 4.1, to get to within \epsilon > 0 of the best possible risk, with probability at least 1 - \delta, we need 
n \geq \frac{2}{\epsilon^2} \log \left( \frac{2 |\mathcal{F}| }{\delta} \right)
 samples in the training dataset. That is, the sample complexity (i.e. how many samples are needed in the training dataset to achieve the nominal performance level \epsilon with probability at least 1 - \delta) scales like O(\epsilon^{-2}), e.g. 100\times as many training data are required for a 10\times reduction in the generalisation error. This is a typical sample complexity result in settings where data are independently sampled.










TipRemark (Bias-Variance Trade-Off)






Remark 4.2 (Bias-Variance Trade-Off). Theorem 4.1 demonstrates a bias-variance trade-off for the risk: 
\mathcal{R}(f_n) \leq \underbrace{ \left( \min_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(f) \right) }_{\mathrm{bias}} + \underbrace{ \sqrt{ \frac{2}{n} \log \frac{2 |\mathcal{F}| }{\delta} } }_{\mathrm{variance}}
\tag{4.1} Here the first term represents the “irreducible bias” due to the choice of machine learning model \mathcal{F}, while the second term represents the “variance”, meaning the error that is associated with training the machine learning model from a random dataset.
To illustrate the trade-off, suppose we are considering switching to a more flexible machine learning model \mathcal{F}' \supseteq \mathcal{F}. If we switch to \mathcal{F}' then the “bias” term on the right hand side of can only decrease (since we are taking a minimum over a larger set). However, the second term would increase since |\mathcal{F}'| \geq |\mathcal{F}|.
This provides useful insight into empirical risk minimisation; the machine learning model \mathcal{F} should be both “not too rigid” and “not too flexible”.










TipRemark (Loose Bound)






Remark 4.3 (Loose Bound). The union bound in Proof 4.1 was used to keep the proof short, but it is crude; if the elements of \mathcal{F} are similar then the events A_f are unlikely to be mutually exclusive, meaning that the union bound is likely to be a loose bound.

title: 4  Generalisation Error
text:
4.2 Domain Shift
The abstract definition of a supervised learning task in Definition 1.1 has the advantage of being well-posed and amenable to a comprehensive mathematical treatment.
However, in real-world applications of supervised learning, the assumption that we have access to a training dataset consisting of n independent samples from the population distribution P on \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y} is almost never satisfied.
For example, our footfall data from the Queen Victoria Road (cf. Example 1.9) arrive sequentially in time; we are in no real sense “sampling” the time index (or the image itself) from a probability distribution.
This raises a serious philosophical issue:

Are the data that we have gathered up to the present representative of data that we are likely to encounter going forward?

Or, more abstractly:

Are the training data representative of the data that will be encountered when the machine learning model is deployed?

This is the fundamental issue of domain shift in machine learning:







Definition 4.2 (Domain shift) Domain shift describes the error associated to deploying a machine learning model in a setting different to that in which it was trained.




The issue of domain shift has major ethical implications for machine learning (cf. Chapter 7); for instance, a machine learning model for medical diagnostics that is trained only on data from an East Asian patient cohort may not perform as intended when applied to patients with European heritage, due to the important role of genetics in disease progression.
Considering the set-up of Theorem 4.1, the actual risk \mathcal{R}_\star associated with deploying the machine learning model can be bounded as 
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{R}_\star(f_n) \leq \underbrace{ \max_{f \in \mathcal{F}} | \mathcal{R}_\star(f) - \mathcal{R}(f)| }_{\mathrm{domain \; shift}} + \underbrace{ \left( \min_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(f) \right) }_{\mathrm{bias}} + \underbrace{ \sqrt{ \frac{2}{n} \log \frac{2 |\mathcal{F}| }{\delta} } }_{\mathrm{variance}}
\end{align*}
 where the first term captures the extent to which risk \mathcal{R} in the training context differs from the risk \mathcal{R}_\star in deployment.




Bach, Francis. 2024. Learning Theory from First Principles. MIT Press.

title: 5  Online Supervised Learning
text:
5.1 Bandits
Up to this point we have talked about training a machine learning model once, using a fixed dataset, after which the model is deployed for its intended task.
Online learning, on the other hand, updates the machine learning model incrementally as new data arrive, allowing it to adapt to changing patterns in real-time. This helps maintain model relevance in dynamic environments, and is also useful for large or streaming datasets where storing and retraining on all past data is impractical.
To fix ideas, we can precisely formulate an online supervised learning task:
Definition 5.1 is deliberately vague about where the sequence of data-generating distributions P_t might come from; there are two main situations to consider
The simplest example of online machine learning without feedback is called the bandit, which we are going to meet in Section 5.1.
Online machine learning with feedback is such a rich topic that we cannot hope to cover it in this module, but we give a passing nod to reinforcement learning, one of the main methods that address this task, in Section 5.2.
Slot machines are also known pejoratively as one-armed bandits, alluding to the large mechanical levers affixed to the sides of early mechanical machines (cf. Figure 5.1), and to the games’ ability to empty players’ pockets and wallets as thieves would.
At time t the player inserts a coin (say \pounds 1), pulls the lever, and receives a random reward \pounds R_t which has expectation \mu \geq 0 and is independent of all other rewards that have been received. Their average expected reward after playing T rounds is simply the expected reward \mu from the bandit, i.e. 
\mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T R_t \right] = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{E}[R_t] = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mu = \mu ,
 So far, so straightforward. The complication comes in when there is more than one bandit (we call this situation a multi-armed bandit), since the player must then select, at time t, which bandit to play next. This is non-trivial when not all bandits are equal; the expected reward \mu_i from the ith bandit may not be the same as the expected reward \mu_j from another bandit (j \neq i), and the actual values of the \mu_i will be unknown to the player in general. Supposing there are B bandits in total, the aim is then to minimise the regret 
\mu_\star - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T R_t , \qquad \mu_\star = \max_{1 \leq i \leq B} \mu_i ,    
\tag{5.1} where R_t denotes the reward received at time t \in \{1,\dots,T\}. If a player was lucky enough to only play the bandit with highest expected reward \mu_\star, then the player would have no expected regret: 
\mathbb{E}\left[ \mu_\star - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T R_t \right]
= \mu_\star - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{E}[ R_t]
= \mu_\star - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mu_{\star} = 0
 However, only by experimenting with each bandit, and potentially losing money in the process, can the player hope to truly discover which bandit provides the highest expected reward.
Though the terminology is inherited from gambling, multi-arm bandits appear in diverse application areas. For example, in online advertising the advertiser would like to dynamically select which among a selection of different advertisements maximises click-through rates, or in sequential clinical trials one seeks to allocate treatments to maximise patient welfare with only a partial understanding of which treatments are effective at the outset.
Multi-arm bandits can be seen as a special case of the general online supervised learning task (cf. Definition 5.1) by taking \mathcal{X} = \emptyset, \mathcal{Z} \in \{1,\dots,B\} indexes the bandits that can be played, \mathbf{y}_t = (R_t^{(1)} , \dots , R_t^{(B)}) are the rewards that would have been paid by each bandit at time t, and L(\mathbf{y}_t , f) = - [\mathbf{y}_t]_f = - R_t^{(f)}. In particular, the regret Equation 5.1 is consistent with the notion of regret that we saw earlier in Equation 3.4.
Although there is some redundancy in talking about both losses and rewards, the “reward” terminology feels much more natural in the bandit context, so we will use it.
The reason that multi-arm bandits are non-trivial is because the player must balance two competing objectives; exploration, to find out which bandit provides the highest expected reward, and exploitation, to repeatedly play the machine that is believed to provide the highest expected reward. This is known as an exploration-exploitation trade-off.
Let’s examine the two edge cases in turn:

title: 5  Online Supervised Learning
text:
TipRemark (Contextual Bandit)






Remark 5.1 (Contextual Bandit). A natural extension of the multi-arm bandit, which we will not consider in this module, is when the output from the bandit depends also on observable covariates \mathbf{x}_t \in \mathcal{X}.
For example, in a clinical trial we may know that patients with a specific genetic trait are more likely to respond well to a particular treatment, and we can use this information to help decide to which arm of the trial they are assigned.
This is known as a contextual bandit, with \mathbf{x}_t representing the context.










Figure 5.1: A row of classical bandit machines, on display at Wookey Hole Caves in Somerset, England. Since there are four bandits, we call this setting a 4-armed bandit.. [source]






5.1.1 Pure Exploration
If we want to learn as much as we can about the vector \bm{\mu} = (\mu_1,\dots,\mu_B) of expected rewards, then an intuitively reasonable strategy is to spend an equal amount of time playing each bandit. The expected regret is then 
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}\left[ \mu_\star - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T R_t  \right] & = \mu_\star - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{E}[R_t] \\
& = \mu_\star - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^B \mu_i \\
& = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^B (\mu_\star - \mu_i)
\end{align*}
 which does not vanish (assuming the \mu_i are not all equal) as T \rightarrow \infty; we always have some regret if we play a pure exploitation strategy!


5.1.2 Pure Exploitation
The opposite of exploration is to repeatedly play the machine that we believe has the highest expected reward. Of course, we know nothing at the outset, so let’s suppose we allocate the first T_0 attempts to performing some form of exploration, enabling us to estimate the vector \bm{\mu} of expected rewards from these data, say using \hat{\bm{\mu}}. Thereafter we will continue to play any bandit which maximises i \mapsto \hat{\mu}_i. Since the exploration dataset has finite size T_0, we cannot expect \hat{\bm{\mu}} to be in exact agreement with \bm{\mu}; as such, there is a positive probability that 
\argmax_{1 \leq i \leq B} \hat{\mu}_i \notin \argmax_{1 \leq i \leq B} \mu_i ,
 and we will go on to indefinitely play a sub-optimal bandit. Let \gamma = 1 if this event occurs, and otherwise \gamma = 0. Let \rho = \mathbb{E}[\gamma] be the probability of this event, and let 
\Delta = \mu_\star - \max\left\{ \mu_i : \mu_i \neq \mu_\star \right\}
 be the difference in expectation between the best bandit(s) and the second best bandit(s). Then 
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}\left[ \mu_\star - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T R_t  \right]
    & = \underbrace{ \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T_0} \mathbb{E}[ \mu_\star -  R_t ] }_{\rightarrow 0 \text{ as } T \rightarrow \infty} + \underbrace{ \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=T_0+1}^T \mathbb{E}[ \mu_\star - R_t]  }_{(*)}
\end{align*}
 where, using the tower property of conditional expectation, 
\begin{align*}
    (\star) & = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t = T_0 + 1}^T \mathbb{E}[ \mathbb{E}[ \mu_\star - R_t | \gamma] ]
    \geq \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t = T_0 + 1}^T [ (1 - \rho) \times 0 + \rho \times \Delta ]
    = \frac{\rho}{T} \sum_{t=T_0+1}^T \Delta
\end{align*}
 which does not vanish as T \rightarrow \infty. Thus we are not much better off than the pure exploration strategy in Section 5.1.1; we have non-vanishing expected regret.


5.1.3 \epsilon-greedy
From Section 5.1.1 and Section 5.1.2, it is intuitively clear that neither pure exploration or pure exploitation are satisfactory; given an infinite number of attempts, we ought to be able to eventually identify the bandit paying the highest expected reward and then exploit it. That is, there ought to be a mixed strategy, involving both exploration and exploitation, for which we have asymptotically vanishing regret. Such strategies do indeed exist and are not unique; in this section we consider a particularly simple idea called the \epsilon-greedy method.
The idea behind \epsilon-greedy is that we eventually want to have accurate estimates for the vector \bm{\mu} of average rewards, but we only want to devote a small proportion \epsilon of our playing to achieve this goal.
To operationalise this, we can imagine that at each time t we “flip an \epsilon coin” to decide whether to play a bandit selected uniformly at random (i.e. with probability \epsilon we explore by playing a random bandit), or to play the bandit we currently believe to be the best (i.e. with probability 1 - \epsilon we exploit our current knowledge to play what we believe is most likely to be the best bandit).
Let’s calculate our expected regret under the \epsilon-greedy method. Let \gamma_t be the event that our belief about which is the best bandit is incorrect at time t and let \rho_t = \mathbb{E}[\gamma_t]. Using again the tower property of conditional expectation, this time we derive an upper bound 
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}\left[ \mu_\star - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T R_t  \right]
        & = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{E}[\mu_\star - \mathbb{E}[R_t | \gamma_t]  ]
        \leq \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \rho_t \Delta
\end{align*}
 which vanishes as T \rightarrow \infty whenever \rho_t \rightarrow 0 as t \rightarrow \infty. In other words, as long as we eventually learn which is the best bandit, we will have asymptotically zero regret.
A simple strategy to learn the best bandit is to let \hat{\mu}_i be the average of the rewards that we have obtained from the ith bandit at time t; from Hoeffding’s inequality 4.1 we know that each \hat{\mu}_i converges to \mu_i in probability as the total number of plays of the ith bandit is increased, and from this we can deduce that \rho_t, the probability of selecting a sub-optimal bandit, becomes vanishingly small.

title: 5  Online Supervised Learning
text:
5.2 Reinforcement Learning
The challenge of online supervised learning is markedly increased when our actions at time t can affect future outcomes; i.e. in the presence of feedback. An important example of this is a Markov decision process, where the states (\mathbf{x}_t)_{t \geq 1} evolve as a Markov chain, and \mathbf{x}_{t+1} is allowed to depend on the action f(\mathbf{x}_t) that we take at time t.
The study of how to select a policy f(\cdot) to minimise regret is called reinforcement learning. All of the previous considerations from Section 5.1 apply here; we also are faced with an exploration-exploitation trade-off, since we want to both find and exploit an optimal policy f(\cdot).







Example 5.1 (AlphaGo) Go, an abstract strategy board game for two players in which the aim is to fence off more territory than the opponent, was invented in China more than 2,500 years ago (Figure 5.2). A decade or so ago many people believed that computers would not be able to compete with the most skilled human players at Go.
This was not an unreasonable belief; the most powerful chess engines were exploiting tree search to explore the consequences of a large number of moves several steps ahead, but by comparison the combinatorial complexity of Go would render tree search impractical.
This all changed with AlphaGo, which in 2016 defeated one of the world’s top professional players Silver et al. (2016).
AlphaGo was in effect a demonstration of the potential of reinforcement learning, showing how this enables a computer to evaluate board positions and anticipate future moves with remarkable precision.
Let’s see how this online supervised learning task is formulated:

The state \mathbf{x}_t represents the current configuration of the Go board, including the positions of all black and white stones, whose turn it is, and any additional game-specific information (for Go aficionados, this includes ko situations).
The policy f(\cdot) is constructed using a deep neural network and tells us where to place our next stone on the board1.
The next state \mathbf{x}_{t+1} is obtained from the current state \mathbf{x}_t and the action f(\mathbf{x}_t). For Go this is fully deterministic; placing a stone on a legal point leads to a new board configuration (with any captures resolved).
AlphaGo used a sparse reward, with R_t = 0 for all intermediate moves and either R_t = 1 or –1 at the end of the game, depending on whether the game was won or lost.







Figure 5.2: The first 99 moves in AlphaGo (white) v. Tang Weixing (31 December 2016). [source]







The field of reinforcement learning is moving fast. For example, the performance of AlphaGo has been superseded by a general-purpose machine learning tool for game-playing called MuZero Schrittwieser et al. (2020).




Schrittwieser, Julian, Ioannis Antonoglou, Thomas Hubert, Karen Simonyan, Laurent Sifre, Simon Schmitt, Arthur Guez, et al. 2020. “Mastering Atari, Go, Chess and Shogi by Planning with a Learned Model.” Nature 588 (7839): 604–9.


Silver, David, Aja Huang, Chris J Maddison, Arthur Guez, Laurent Sifre, George Van Den Driessche, Julian Schrittwieser, et al. 2016. “Mastering the Game of Go with Deep Neural Networks and Tree Search.” Nature 529 (7587): 484–89.

title: 5  Online Supervised Learning
text: Of course we are glossing over details here; for example, in AlphaGo a stochastic policy was actually used.↩︎

title: 6  Beyond Supervised Learning
text:
6.1 Unsupervised Learning
This module primarily focuses on supervised learning, meaning that to each input \mathbf{X} there is an associated label \mathbf{Y} that provides information on the quality of the output from a machine learning model f(\mathbf{X}) via the loss function L(\mathbf{Y},f(\mathbf{X})). Supervised learning is mathematically well-defined and amenable to an advanced theoretical treatment; for strong postgraduate students we recommend the recent textbook of Bach (2024).
However, there are other important tasks which cannot be cast as supervised learning, typically because one has no access to labels \mathbf{Y} (unsupervised learning; Section 6.1) or partial access to labels (semi-supervised learning; Section 6.2). One of the most important and interesting unsupervised learning tasks is generative modelling, and we dedicate Section 6.3 to an in-depth look at this task.
Unsupervised learning refers to analysis of unlabelled data to identify patterns, structures, or relationships without any guidance or explicit instructions on the correct output. Instead of relying on predefined categories, the aim is to autonomously discover groupings or hidden structures within the data, often through techniques such as clustering (which we discuss here) or dimensionality reduction (which we discuss in Section 2.1.2.2).
Clustering involves grouping a set of data points into clusters, such that data within the same cluster are more similar to each other than to data in different clusters. This technique is widely applied in areas such as genomics (to identify different genetic populations within a patient cohort), image analysis (to select an appropriate colour palette; cf. Example 6.1), and in commerce (to target advertising to consumers with similar profiles), where understanding the natural groupings of data can support decision-making and insight.
Suppose we have data \{\mathbf{x}_i\}_{i=1}^n \subset \mathbb{R}^d that we wish to divide into k different sub-groups, or clusters1.
That is, to each datum \mathbf{x}_i we seek to associated a label y_i \in \{1,\dots,k\}, such that data with the same label are more similar to each other compared to data with a different label. As an example, we can consider the optimisation task 
\argmin_{y_1,\dots,y_n} \; \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n 1_{y_i = y_j} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j\|^2 ,    
\tag{6.1} where the aim is to select labels \{y_i\}_{i=1}^n for which the sum of squared distances between data in the same cluster is minimised2.
Unfortunately, this is a computationally hard optimisation when n or k are large, because the number of potential label assignments is k^n, meaning that an exhaustive search can be impractical.
A simple and popular heuristic algorithm for approximately solving Equation 6.1 is called k-means. The basic idea is that each cluster is represented by a centroid \mathbf{c}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d, which is the mean location of the data within that cluster, and the location of the centroids are optimised, together with the cluster assignments, so that a surrogate loss function 
L \equiv L(\{\mathbf{c}_i\}_{i=1}^k , \{y_j\}_{j=1}^n) = \sum_{j=1}^n \| \mathbf{x}_j - \mathbf{c}_{y_j} \|^2
 is approximately minimised.
Let’s randomly initialise the centroids at some values \{\mathbf{c}_i\}_{i=1}^k \subset \mathbb{R}^d. Then we perform coordinate descent on L; i.e., the following optimisation steps are iteratively performed:
These two steps are repeated until the centroids no longer change significantly, or a predefined number of iterations is reached. Once the algorithm has terminated, the final cluster assignments are reported.

title: 6  Beyond Supervised Learning
text:
Minimise L with respect to \{y_j\}_{j=1}^n while holding \{\mathbf{c}_i\}_{i=1}^k fixed: It is straightforward to see that this is achieved when each data point \mathbf{x}_j is assigned to the nearest centroid:
y_j \in \argmin_{i} \|\mathbf{x}_j - \mathbf{c}_i \|^2
Here, y_j is the index of the centroid to which data point \mathbf{x}_j is assigned (if there is more than one nearest centroid, just pick one at random for the assignment).
Minimise L with respect to \{\mathbf{c}_i\}_{i=1}^k while holding \{y_j\}_{j=1}^n fixed: Since L is a quadratic function of each \mathbf{c}_i, we can differentiate L and solve for the unique stationary point:

\begin{aligned}
    \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{c}_i} & = \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{c}_i}  \sum_{j=1}^n \| \mathbf{x}_j - \mathbf{c}_{y_j} \|^2 \\
    & = \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{c}_i}  \sum_{j=1}^n \mathbb{1}_{\{y_j = i\}} \| \mathbf{x}_j - \mathbf{c}_i \|^2 \\
    & =  \sum_{j=1}^n \mathbb{1}_{\{y_j = i\}} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{c}_i}  \| \mathbf{x}_j - \mathbf{c}_i \|^2 \\
    & =  \sum_{j=1}^n \mathbb{1}_{\{y_j = i\}}  [ - 2 (\mathbf{x}_j - \mathbf{c}_i) ] \\
    & = - 2 \sum_{j=1}^n \mathbb{1}_{\{y_j = i\}}  \mathbf{x}_j + 2 \sum_{j=1}^n \mathbb{1}_{\{y_j = i\}} \mathbf{c}_i
\end{aligned}

and so
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{c}_i} = \mathbf{0} \implies \mathbf{c}_i = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^n \mathbb{1}_{\{y_j = i\}} \mathbf{x}_j}{\sum_{j=1}^n \mathbb{1}_{\{y_j = i\}}}
i.e., \mathbf{c}_i is taken to be the mean location of the data currently assigned to the ith cluster.









Example 6.1 (Colour quantisation) In computer graphics, k-means clustering is frequently used for colour quantisation in image compression. By reducing the number of colours used to represent an image, file sizes can be significantly reduced without a noticeable loss of visual quality.
For example, consider the image of a flower with millions of colours in the left panel of Figure 6.1. By applying k-means clustering with k = 16 the image can be represented using a limited palette of only 16 colours, resulting in a compressed version that requires less storage space.













Figure 6.1: An application of k-means clustering to identify k = 16 representative colours than can be used to compress the image of a flower in the left panel. (For illustrative purposes the blue colour channel has been removed.) The blue lines indicate the cluster boundaries; i.e. the locations that lie exactly half way between the two nearest centroids (blue circles). The regions circumscribed by the blue lines are called Voronoi cells. [source]



It is worth emphasising that k-means clustering is not guaranteed to solve Equation 6.1; it is sensitive to the initial placement of centroids and may result in different clusters for different initialisations. Therefore, it is often run multiple times with different initial seeds to find a stable solution.
Additionally, the value of k (the number of clusters) should be chosen carefully, and several heuristics have been developed. This module will not discuss selecting k, but you can read about different strategies on Wikipedia if you are interested.

title: 6  Beyond Supervised Learning
text:
6.2 Semi-supervised Learning
Suppose that we wish to undertake a supervised learning task (cf. Definition 1.1) but unfortunately only a small number of the labels \mathbf{y}_i have been recorded in the training dataset.
This is called a semi-supervised learning task. In an extreme case, suppose we with to perform binary classification (i.e. into two classes) of data based on their covariates \{\mathbf{x}_i\}_{i=1}^n \subset \mathbb{R}^d, but only two data have their true labels recorded.

Can anything at all be achieved?

Surprisingly, the answer is sometimes “yes”, and the key idea here is called the manifold hypothesis:







Definition 6.1 (Manifold hypothesis) The manifold hypothesis suggests that possibly high-dimensional data \{\mathbf{x}_i\}_{i=1}^n \subset \mathbb{R}^d can be effectively represented in a lower-dimensional space, most often a smooth manifold embedded in \mathbb{R}^d.











Example 6.2 (Manifold hypothesis for image data) For example, images of handwritten digits (see Figure 2.11) may lie close to a low-dimensional manifold that captures most of the variations of those digits, despite their high-dimensional pixel representation; see Figure 6.2.














Figure 6.2: An illustration of how images of hand-drawn digits can be mapped onto a lower-dimensional manifold without significant loss of information content.
[source]



The unlabelled data are therefore not useless in cases where the manifold hypothesis holds; they can be leveraged to learn the manifold, reducing the dimension (and therefore the difficulty) of the learning task. This is closely related to the concept of featurisation, discussed in Section 2.2.4.







Example 6.3 (Label propagation for a binary classification task) Figure 6.3 illustrates a setting in which we can perform binary classification when only a handful of labels are recorded in the training dataset. The term label propagation is sometimes used to capture the idea that information from labelled data spreads to unlabelled data based on their proximity on the manifold.










Figure 6.3: Illustrating supervised, semi-supervised, and unsupervised learning.
[source]



It is common to assume that the manifold hypothesis holds in tasks such as image classification, natural language processing and medical diagnosis, where data are typically high-dimensional. In many real-world problems, data have a much lower effective dimension than their notional dimension (cf. Section 2.1.2.2), and modern machine learning models are often designed to discover and exploit this underlying low-dimensional manifold.

title: 6  Beyond Supervised Learning
text:
6.3 Generative Modelling
One of the most important tasks in unsupervised learning is generative modelling; given a dataset \{\mathbf{x}_i\}_{i=1}^n \subset \mathbb{R}^d we seek a probability distribution P \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d) for which (a) the \mathbf{x}_i “look like typical samples” from P, and (b) further “new” samples can be generated from P, which are distinct from those \mathbf{x}_i in the dataset. Of course, you have seen this task already in MAS2901 or MAS8601 when you used a method like maximum likelihood to fit a statistical model (e.g. a normal distribution) to a given dataset.
The main distinction between classical statistical modelling and generative modelling in machine learning is the complexity of the dataset; for example, each \mathbf{x}_i could represent the image of a cat, and we want to learn a probability distribution P for which “typical” samples from P look like cats; a normal distribution is clearly going to be inadequate for this task. This poses two main challenges to “traditional” statistical modelling; we cannot expect to write down a suitable statistical model by hand, and even if we could then it may not make sense to train such a model using maximum likelihood:






TipRemark (Failure of maximum likelihood under the manifold hypothesis )






Remark 6.1 (Failure of maximum likelihood under the manifold hypothesis ). Suppose we are in a setting where data \{\mathbf{x}_i\}_{i=1}^n lie on a lower-dimensional manifold M \subset \mathbb{R}^d (for example, M is the manifold of images of cats, a subspace of the space of all images; see Definition 6.1). Suppose further that we have a “good” parametric statistical model P_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} that is aware of the manifold; that is, the density p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}) is zero for \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d \setminus M (we say that P_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} is supported on M). Then the density p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\cdot) must necessarily take the value \infty on M, meaning that the maximum likelihood estimator is not well defined3.




Despite the apparent challenges of generative modelling, we now have machine learning models and ways to train them that can perform astonishingly well at this task; see Figure 6.4. In this section we are going to learn more about modern generative models (Section 6.3.1) and how they are trained (Section 6.3.2).






Figure 6.4: Illustrating a generative model. [source]




6.3.1 Generative Models
A natural first question is:

What sort of model could we write down that has the capacity to generate realistic samples?

One can keep in mind image data as motivation, but the concept of a generative model is general. As such, we distinguish at a high level between the two main approaches:







Definition 6.2 (Simulation-based models) Recall that sometimes it is easier to reason with random variables than with probability distributions (cf. Recap 1.6). To this end, let f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} : \mathbb{R}^c \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^d be a parametric function and define a random variable by 
\mathbf{X} = f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{Z}),
 where \mathbf{Z} is a simple random variable that can be easily sampled, such as 
\mathbf{Z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}).
 The distribution of \mathbf{X} then defines a generative model P_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}, parametrised by \boldsymbol{\theta}. For obvious reasons, such a generative model is called simulation-based.











Definition 6.3 (Energy-based models) Alternatively, we may proceed based on densities and define the density of our generative model P_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} as 
p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})
\propto
\exp\!\big(- f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})\big),
 for some function f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} : \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, which again could be a neural network. Such a generative model is called energy-based because of an analogy from physics, in which P_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} is viewed as a Gibbs measure and f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}) corresponds to the energy of the configuration \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d.




Simulation-based models are easy to sample from by design, but depending on f_{\bm{\theta}} it can be hard to compute quantities relating to the density function of the model, for example as you would need for maximum likelihood. On the other hand, energy-based models provide direct access to the density function by design (up to a normalisation constant), but it can require complicated numerical methods to sample from the model (such as Markov chain Monte Carlo, which you may have met in MAS3929 or MAS8600).
In either case, the expressive capacity of the generative model depends on the expressive capacity of the function f_{\bm{\theta}}; for challenging applications f_{\bm{\theta}} may need to be extremely flexible, for the example in Figure 6.4 the function f_{\bm{\theta}} was a deep neural network.


6.3.2 Training Generative Models

6.3.2.1 Adversarial Training
Simulation-based models are conveniently designed for generating samples, but do not provide explicit access to the density function p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (or derived quantities, such as its gradient). As such, ideas such as maximum likelihood cannot easily be implemented, irrespective of how well these methods for training may work (cf. Remark 6.1). Instead, to guide the selection of the model parameters \boldsymbol{\theta}, we need another way to judge whether samples \mathbf{X} from the model P_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} are “similar” or not to those of the training dataset \{\mathbf{x}_i\}_{i=1}^n. How are we going to achieve this?
Taking image data as an example, it does not make sense to compare \mathbf{X} and \mathbf{x}_i through Euclidean distance \lVert \mathbf{X} - \mathbf{x}_i \rVert because we do not expect our artificially generated image \mathbf{X} to be similar pixel-by-pixel to an image \mathbf{x}_i in the training dataset. (If it were, we would have simply memorised the training dataset, which is not in the spirit of fitting a generative model.) What makes a cat picture a cat picture is not the pixel-by-pixel information content; it is the appearance of fur, whiskers, and the general air of disdain. How can we capture these aspects of \mathbf{X}?
The solution is to recall the concept of featurisation. Consider a feature map (cf. Definition 2.4) 
\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\phi_1(\mathbf{x}) \\
\vdots \\
\phi_p(\mathbf{x})
\end{bmatrix}
 and the associated discrepancy 
D_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(P_{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
=
\left\|
\int
\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})\, p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}) \, \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}
-
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_i)
\right\|.
\tag{6.2}
If we were able to find features \phi_1, \dots, \phi_p that codify the “essence” of cats, then we could seek the parameter values \boldsymbol{\theta} for which the discrepancy D_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(P_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) is minimised. That is, we could ensure that the samples \mathbf{X} from our generative model P_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} most closely resemble the dataset in the respects that count.
For example, if \phi_1(\mathbf{x}) is whisker length and \phi_2(\mathbf{x}) is squared whisker length, then minimising D_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(P_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) would amount to matching the first and second moment (equivalently, mean and variance) of whisker length between our generative model and the dataset. But how could we hope to find features that are so specifically engineered to capture the relevant aspects of the dataset?
The key, as we have already seen (cf. Section 2.1.2), is to use data-driven features, and one way to do this is to select features adversarially: 
D_{\Phi}(P_{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
=
\sup_{\boldsymbol{\phi} \in \Phi}
D_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(P_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}).
\tag{6.3}
Here the supremum is taken over some appropriate set \Phi of possible feature functions \boldsymbol{\phi}.
We can interpret Equation 6.3 as a two-player game:
Player 1 simulates artificial samples from their model P_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}, and Player 2 has to pick features \boldsymbol{\phi} that will help them to detect which samples are artificial and which are real. Typically we do not want to employ a human to act as Player 2, so a natural idea is to replace Player 2 by a classifier whose feature map \boldsymbol{\phi} can be trained to maximally distinguish between the artificial and real samples; for example, \boldsymbol{\phi} can be a deep neural network4.
The resulting framework for training simulation-based models is called a generative adversarial network (or GAN). Until around 2020, generative adversarial networks were among the state of the art for generating realistic images; the example in Figure 6.4 was produced in this way in 2021. However, a step change in generative model performance occurred around 2020, and the state of the art are now (extensions of) energy-based models, as we will discuss next.






TipRemark (The power of adversarial training)






Remark 6.2 (The power of adversarial training). Adversarial training of a machine learning model is a powerful idea that enables simpler or pre-trained machine learning models to assist with the training of more sophisticated machine learning models.
For example, although AlphaGo 5.1 was initially trained on historical game data, it was honed and refined by playing millions of games against itself.






6.3.2.2 Score Matching
The challenge of working with energy-based models p_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}) \propto \exp( - f_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}) ) is that the normalisation constant 
\begin{align*}
    Z_{\bm{\theta}} = \int \exp( - f_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}) ) \mathrm{d} \mathbf{x}
\end{align*}
 is in general an analytically intractable integral. This is a real problem; if we wanted to find the parameters \bm{\theta} that maximise the likelihood we cannot simply find the \bm{\theta} that maximises 
\bm{\theta} \mapsto \prod_{i=1}^n \exp( - f_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_i))
 because there is also a \bm{\theta} dependence in the neglected normalisation constant. However, there is a clever way to circumvent working directly with this normalising constant, which is to notice that its Stein score can be computed without the normalising constant:







Definition 6.4 (Stein score) Let P be a probability distribution with density p on \mathbb{R}^d. The Stein score of P is 
s_P(\mathbf{x}) = (\nabla \log p)(\mathbf{x})
 where here \nabla denotes the gradient with respect to the \mathbf{x} argument.




The Stein score is names after Charles Stein (1920-2016), who popularised the use of the Stein score as a theoretical tool (initially for proving central limit theorems) in the 1970s; computational and machine learning applications of the Stein score are a more recent development. For an energy-based model P_{\bm{\theta}} the Stein score is 
s_{P_{\bm{\theta}}}(\mathbf{x}) =  (\nabla \log p)(\mathbf{x}) = \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} \{ - f_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}) - \log Z_{\bm{\theta}} \} = - \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})   
\tag{6.4} which can be computed without access to the intractable normalising constant Z_{\bm{\theta}}. Critically, a Stein score s_P fully characterises the associated distribution P:







Proposition 6.1 Let P and Q have Stein scores s_P and s_Q. Then s_P and s_Q are everywhere equal if and only if P and Q are equal.










NoteProof (Not Examinable)






Proof 6.1 (Not Examinable). The equality of Stein scores is equivalent to the constancy of the ratio of the densities p and q for P and Q, since 
s_P(\mathbf{x}) - s_Q(\mathbf{x}) = \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} \log \left( \frac{p(\mathbf{x})}{q(\mathbf{x})} \right) .
 Further, the ratio p/q is constant if and only if p and q are equal, since p/q = C if and only if p(\mathbf{x}) = C q(\mathbf{x}) for all \mathbf{x}, and since both p and q integrate to 1 this situation can only occur when C = 1.




Proposition 6.1 suggests a convenient approach to training an energy-based model P_{\bm{\theta}}; we can try to “match” the Stein score of P_{\bm{\theta}} to the Stein score of the true data-generating distribution. However, we do not have access to the Stein score of the data-generating distribution, we only have a training dataset \{\mathbf{x}_i\}_{i=1}^n consisting of samples from it.

How then can we proceed?

The solution is essentially a clever application of integration-by-parts5, due to Hyvärinen (2005).







Proposition 6.2 (Manipulating the Stein score) Let P and Q be distributions on \mathbb{R}^d with densities p and q, respectively. Assuming q(\mathbf{x}) (\nabla \log p)(\mathbf{x}) vanishes (uniformly) as \|\mathbf{x}\| \rightarrow \infty, 
\int \| s_P(\mathbf{x}) - s_Q(\mathbf{x}) \|^2 \mathrm{d}Q(\mathbf{x}) = \int \|(\nabla \log p)(\mathbf{x})\|^2 + 2 (\Delta \log p)(\mathbf{x}) \; \mathrm{d}Q(\mathbf{x}) + C_Q   
\tag{6.5} where C_Q depends on Q but not on P.










NoteProof (Not Examinable)






Proof 6.2 (Not Examinable). From the divergence theorem (i.e. multivariate integration-by-parts; see e.g. MSP2801), 
\begin{align*}
    \int \langle \nabla \log p , \nabla \log q \rangle \; \mathrm{d}Q & = \int \left\langle (\nabla \log p)(\mathbf{x}) , \frac{(\nabla q)(\mathbf{x})}{q(\mathbf{x})} \right\rangle \; q(\mathbf{x}) \; \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x} \\
    & = \int \langle (\nabla \log p)(\mathbf{x}) , (\nabla q)(\mathbf{x}) \rangle \; \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x} \\
    & = \int q(\mathbf{x}) (\Delta \log p)(\mathbf{x}) \; \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x} \\
    & = \int (\Delta \log p)(\mathbf{x}) \; \mathrm{d}Q(\mathbf{x})
\end{align*}
 where the boundary term that appears in integration-by-parts vanishes since we assumed q(\mathbf{x}) (\nabla \log p)(\mathbf{x}) \rightarrow \mathbf{0} uniformly as \|\mathbf{x}\| \rightarrow \infty. Thus 
\begin{align*}
    \int \| s_P(\mathbf{x}) - s_Q(\mathbf{x}) \|^2 \mathrm{d}Q(\mathbf{x}) & = \int \underbrace{ \langle \nabla \log p , \nabla \log p \rangle }_{\|(\nabla \log p)(\mathbf{x})\|^2} - 2 \langle \nabla \log p , \nabla \log q \rangle + \underbrace{ \langle \nabla \log q , \nabla \log q \rangle }_{\text{independent of $P$}} \; \mathrm{d}Q \\
    & = \int \|(\nabla \log p)(\mathbf{x})\|^2 + 2 (\Delta \log p)(\mathbf{x}) \; \mathrm{d}Q(\mathbf{x}) + C_Q
\end{align*}
 as required.




That is, we can indeed train our energy-based model by matching Stein scores, and we do this by minimising the right hand side of Equation 6.5 from Proposition 6.2 where P is P_{\bm{\theta}} and where Q is replaced by the empirical distribution of the dataset:







Definition 6.5 (Score matching) Given a dataset \{\mathbf{x}_i\}_{i=1}^n and a generative model P_{\bm{\theta}}, the score matching estimator is 
\argmin_{\bm{\theta} \in \Theta} \quad \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \|(\nabla \log p_{\bm{\theta}})(\mathbf{x}_i)\|^2 + 2 (\Delta \log p_{\bm{\theta}})(\mathbf{x}_i)   
\tag{6.6}




The quantities appearing in Definition 6.5 can indeed be calculated for energy-based models, due to Equation 6.4. Score matching and maximum likelihood estimation happen to yield the same result when training a normal generative model (cf. Question 18), but in general these objectives can be different.
Score matching has been around since at least Hyvärinen (2005), and has been widely used in statistics to circumvent intractable normalisation constants Z_{\bm{\theta}}.
However, the optimisation landscape for score matching in Equation 6.6 can be difficult to navigate, and this limited its potential.
A breakthrough occurred around 2020, when Ho, Jain, and Abbeel (2020) and Song, Meng, and Ermon (n.d.) had the idea of constructing a sequence of relaxed optimisation problems, where one first solves an easier problem and leverages the solution to inform the next problem in the sequence, eventually enabling the original problem to be solved:







Example 6.4 (Denoising diffusions) Let P_0 be the distribution from which the dataset \{\mathbf{x}_i\}_{i=1}^n are considered to have been sampled. Construct a sequence (P_t)_{t > 0} of probability distributions, such that if \mathbf{X}_t \sim P_t and \mathbf{Z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}), then \mathbf{X}_t + (s-t) \mathbf{Z} \sim P_s for all s \geq t (one can interpret such a construction as a diffusion process, but we do not need this detail). Each P_t can be regarded as a noisy version of the data-generating distribution, where we have taken the original data points \mathbf{x}_i and added independent Gaussian noise; see Figure 6.5.
For large t, say t = T, the distribution P_T will be approximately equal to \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},T\mathbf{I}) and the associated Stein score will be approximately - \mathbf{x} / T, which can be easily matched using e.g. a linear model. The crucial observation is that the Stein score function of P_s is easier to match compared to the Stein score function of P_t whenever s \geq t. Thus we can start by matching the Stein score for P_T and gradually work backward until we have an accurate approximation to the Stein score of P_0. This idea has become known as denoising, referring to working backward from the noisy P_T to the noiseless P_0. Using this approach, score matching can achieve state-of-the-art performance in complex generative modelling tasks. A prominent example of denoising diffusions is Stable Diffusion, which attracted much attention when it was publicly released by Stability AI in 2022.










Figure 6.5: Illustrating the denoising diffusion generative model. [source]







Bach, Francis. 2024. Learning Theory from First Principles. MIT Press.


Ho, Jonathan, Ajay Jain, and Pieter Abbeel. 2020. “Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33: 6840–51.


Hyvärinen, A. 2005. “Estimation of Non-Normalized Statistical Models by Score Matching.” Journal of Machine Learning Research 6: 695.


Song, Jiaming, Chenlin Meng, and Stefano Ermon. n.d. “Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models.” In International Conference on Learning Representations.

title: 7  Ethics of Machine Learning
text:
Now that you are well-versed in the mathematical and statistical foundations of machine learning, we need to confront the elephant in the room; the serious ethical questions that can arise from deployment of powerful machine learning tools in the real world.
Issue 7.1
Issue 7.1
This is not an exhaustive exploration of ethical issues associated with machine learning and AI, but it serves to indicate the depth and breadth of this topic. An important learning outcome, which is examinable, is to be able to highlight and explain some possible ethical considerations associated with deployment of a machine learning model in a given context (cf. Question 19).

title: 8  Introduction to PyTorch
text:
8.2 Introduction to Python
Python is a high-level, general-purpose programming language that has become the de facto standard for machine learning and data science. Its popularity stems from its readable syntax, extensive ecosystem of libraries, and strong community support.
For this course, we will use Python alongside several key libraries:

NumPy for numerical computing and array operations
Matplotlib for data visualisation
PyTorch for building and training neural networks
Pandas for data manipulation


8.2.1 Running Python
There are several ways to run Python code:

Locally — install Python on your own machine via Anaconda or Python.org
In the cloud — use a hosted environment like Google Colab (recommended for this course)
On university computers — Python is pre-installed in the computing labs



8.2.2 Why Google Colab?
For this course, we recommend using Google Colab, a free cloud-based Jupyter notebook environment provided by Google. Colab offers several advantages:

No installation required — runs entirely in your browser
Free GPU access — essential for training neural networks efficiently
Pre-installed libraries — NumPy, Matplotlib, PyTorch, and many others are ready to use
Google Drive integration — easily save and share your work
Collaboration — share notebooks like Google Docs



8.2.3 Getting started with Colab
To run any notebook from this course in Colab:

Click the “Open in Colab” badge at the top of the notebook page
Sign in with your Google account (university or personal)
The notebook will open in a new tab, ready to run

Alternatively, you can upload any .ipynb file directly to Colab via File → Upload notebook.


8.2.4 Colab basics
A Colab notebook consists of cells, which can be either:

Code cells — contain Python code; run with Shift+Enter or the play button
Text cells — contain Markdown for explanations and notes

Some useful keyboard shortcuts:
