  Understand stochastic gradient descent Stochastic Gradient Descent and how it differs from gradient descent Gradient Descent. 



Motivation
In gradient descent Gradient Descent, each update requires computing

\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{R}_n(f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
=
\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (\cdots),

which involves all n data points.
For large datasets, this is computationally expensive.



Key Idea
Stochastic gradient descent Stochastic Gradient Descent replaces the full gradient with an approximation using a random subset (minibatch):

\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{R}_n(f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
\approx
\frac{1}{m}
\sum_{j=1}^m
\nabla_2 L(\mathbf{y}_{i_j}, f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i_j}))
\,
\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i_j}).




Update Rule

\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1}
=
\boldsymbol{\theta}_t
-
\epsilon \, G_t(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t),

where G_t is a stochastic gradient.



Key Properties

G_t is an unbiased estimate of the true gradient: 
\mathbb{E}[G_t(\boldsymbol{\theta})] = \nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta})

introduces noise into the updates
cheaper per iteration than full gradient descent




Trade-off

Smaller minibatch size m:

faster computation
higher variance (noisier updates)

Larger m:

more accurate gradient
higher computational cost





Key Differences from Gradient Descent



Gradient Descent
SGD




Uses all data
Uses minibatches


Accurate gradient
Noisy gradient


Expensive per step
Cheap per step






Key Points

SGD approximates the gradient using random subsets of data.
It is much more scalable than full gradient descent.
Updates are noisy but efficient.
It is the standard method used in practice.






  Understand the convergence of stochastic gradient descent 3.2 (statement and interpretation only). 



Result (Informal)
For a convex objective F, stochastic gradient descent produces iterates (\boldsymbol{\theta}_t) such that

\frac{1}{T}
\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}
\mathbb{E}[F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)]
-
F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_\star)

is small for large T.



Interpretation

On average, SGD gets close to the optimal value.
Convergence is similar to gradient descent 3.1, but:

includes expectation due to randomness;
reflects noisy updates.





Key Insight

SGD behaves like gradient descent on average.
Noise does not prevent convergence, but affects accuracy.




Role of Learning Rate

Same trade-off as gradient descent:

too large → unstable;
too small → slow.





Key Takeaway

SGD converges for convex problems under mild conditions.
It provides a theoretical justification for using noisy gradients.




Key Points

SGD converges in expectation.
Noise is introduced but controlled.
Larger T improves performance.
Similar guarantees to gradient descent, but stochastic.

   Understand automatic differentiation Automatic Differentiation . 



Core Idea
Automatic differentiation Automatic Differentiation  is a computational method for efficiently evaluating derivatives such as

\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{R}_n(f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}).

It underpins modern machine learning frameworks (e.g. PyTorch, JAX).



Why It Is Needed
Training methods such as:

gradient descent Gradient Descent
stochastic gradient descent Stochastic Gradient Descent

require repeated computation of gradients.
For complex models (e.g. neural networks Neural Networks), computing these derivatives by hand is impractical.



Key Property
Automatic differentiation computes derivatives:

exactly (up to numerical precision);
efficiently, even for very complex functions.




Comparison with Numerical Differentiation
Finite-difference methods approximate derivatives:

f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x+\delta) - f(x-\delta)}{2\delta}.

However, these:

are approximate;
can be numerically unstable;
are computationally expensive in high dimensions.




Why Automatic Differentiation Is Better

avoids approximation error;
scales well to high-dimensional parameter spaces;
enables efficient training of large models.




Key Points

Automatic differentiation computes gradients exactly and efficiently.
It is essential for training modern machine learning models.
It is superior to numerical differentiation in both accuracy and scalability.

text:
Chapter 4 - Generalisation Error
Chapter 4 4  Generalisation Error studies how well a trained machine learning model 1.2 performs on new data.
The central object of study is the generalisation error, which measures the gap between the performance of a trained model and the best possible model in the class (cf. risk 1.3).
This chapter introduces:

the definition and intuition behind generalisation error;
 basic generalisation error bounds for empirical risk minimisation Empirical Risk Minimisation;
 related concepts such as sample complexity and the bias–variance trade-off;
the practical issue of domain shift Domain Shift.

With the exception of the basic intuition, the mathematical analysis in this chapter is examinable for MAS8607 students only.


  Understand the definition and intuition of the generalisation error 4.1. 



Definition
The generalisation error 4.1 is

\mathcal{R}(f_n) - \min_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(f),

where:

\mathcal{R}(f) is the risk 1.3 (performance on the true data distribution);
f_n is the trained model (e.g. from empirical risk minimisation Empirical Risk Minimisation);
\mathcal{F} is the model class.




Intuition

\mathcal{R}(f_n) = how well your trained model performs on new data;
\min_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(f) = the best possible performance achievable within the model class.

So the generalisation error measures:

how far your trained model is from the best possible model in \mathcal{F}.




Why It Exists
Generalisation error arises because:

we only observe a finite dataset;
we optimise the empirical risk 1.4, not the true risk;
the empirical risk is only an approximation of the population risk.




Key Properties

Generalisation error is always non-negative;
It depends on:

the model class \mathcal{F};
the amount of data n;
the training procedure.





Key Interpretation

Small generalisation error ⇒ model is close to optimal.
Large generalisation error ⇒ model is suboptimal (e.g. due to overfitting or poor model choice).




Key Points

Generalisation error measures the gap to the best possible model.
It arises from finite data and approximate optimisation.
It is the central quantity in evaluating machine learning models.






   Understand Hoeffding’s inequality 4.1. Note: you are not expected to be remember this result for the exam or its proof. 



Statement
Let Z_1, \dots, Z_n be independent random variables with mean \mu and values in [0,1]. Then for any t > 0,

\mathbb{P}\left(
\left|
\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i - \mu
\right|
\geq t
\right)
\leq
2 \exp(-2 n t^2).




Intuition

The sample average 
\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i
 concentrates around the true mean \mu.
Large deviations from \mu become exponentially unlikely as n increases.




Why It Matters

Gives a high-probability bound on estimation error.
Key tool for analysing:

empirical risk 1.4 vs

population risk 1.3.





Key Behaviour

Larger n ⇒ tighter concentration.
Larger deviation t ⇒ exponentially smaller probability.




Key Points

Hoeffding’s inequality bounds how far averages deviate from expectations.
Probability of large deviations decays exponentially in n.
It is a core tool in generalisation analysis.
This content is examinable for MAS8607 only.






   Understand the generalisation error bound 4.1. 



Statement
For a finite model class \mathcal{F} and loss L \in [0,1], with probability at least 1 - \delta,

\mathcal{R}(f_n) - \min_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(f)
\leq
\sqrt{
\frac{2}{n}
\log \frac{2|\mathcal{F}|}{\delta}
}.




Interpretation
This bounds the generalisation error 4.1.
It shows that:

the trained model is close to the best possible model in \mathcal{F};
the gap shrinks as the dataset size n increases.




Key Dependencies
The bound depends on:

Sample size n
→ larger n ⇒ smaller error
Model size |\mathcal{F}|
→ larger model class ⇒ larger error
Confidence level \delta
→ higher confidence (smaller \delta) ⇒ looser bound




Intuition
There is a trade-off:

More flexible models (large \mathcal{F}):

lower bias
higher variance

Simpler models (small \mathcal{F}):

higher bias
lower variance


This is the bias–variance trade-off.



Key Takeaway

With enough data, empirical risk minimisation performs well.
But performance depends on balancing:

model complexity;
dataset size.





Key Points

Generalisation error decreases as n increases.
Larger model classes increase uncertainty.
Confidence level affects the tightness of the bound.
Captures the bias–variance trade-off.
This content is examinable for MAS8607 only.






   Understand the key steps in the proof 4.1 of the generalisation error bound 4.1. 



What You Are Expected to Know
You are not expected to reproduce the full proof, but you should understand:

the main tools used;
the logical structure of the argument;
how the final bound is obtained.




Step 1 — Apply Hoeffding (pointwise control)
For each fixed model f \in \mathcal{F}:

\mathbb{P}\left(
|\mathcal{R}_n(f) - \mathcal{R}(f)| \geq t
\right)
\leq
2 \exp(-2nt^2).

Interpretation: empirical risk is close to population risk for a fixed model.



Step 2 — Union bound (uniform control)
We want this to hold for all f \in \mathcal{F} simultaneously.
Use the union bound:

\mathbb{P}\left(
\exists f \in \mathcal{F} \text{ such that } |\mathcal{R}_n(f) - \mathcal{R}(f)| \geq t
\right)
\leq
2|\mathcal{F}| e^{-2nt^2}.

Key idea: control worst-case deviation over the whole model class.



Step 3 — Uniform convergence
With high probability:

|\mathcal{R}_n(f) - \mathcal{R}(f)| < t
\quad \text{for all } f \in \mathcal{F}.

This is called uniform convergence.



Step 4 — Relate ERM to optimal model
Let:

f_n = empirical risk minimiser

f_\star = true (population) risk minimiser

Then:

\mathcal{R}(f_n)
\leq
\mathcal{R}_n(f_n) + t
\leq
\mathcal{R}_n(f_\star) + t
\leq
\mathcal{R}(f_\star) + 2t.

Key logic:

empirical ≈ population (uniform convergence)
ERM minimises empirical risk
combine inequalities




Step 5 — Solve for t
Set probability level:

\delta = 2|\mathcal{F}| e^{-2nt^2}
 Rearranging gives: 
t =
\sqrt{
\frac{1}{2n}
\log\left(\frac{2|\mathcal{F}|}{\delta}\right)
}.

Substitute into bound.



Final Result

\mathcal{R}(f_n) - \mathcal{R}(f_\star)
\leq
\sqrt{
\frac{2}{n}
\log \frac{2|\mathcal{F}|}{\delta}
}.




Big Picture
The proof combines:

concentration inequality (Hoeffding)
union bound
ERM optimality

to show:

empirical risk minimisation works because empirical risk approximates population risk uniformly.




Key Points

Hoeffding ⇒ control for a fixed model.
Union bound ⇒ extend to all models.
Uniform convergence ⇒ key concept.
ERM + uniform convergence ⇒ generalisation bound.
You should understand the flow of the argument, not memorise every line.
This content is examinable for MAS8607 only.






  Understand the concept of domain shift Domain Shift and its implications for machine learning performance. 



Core Idea
In theoretical formulations of supervised learning, we assume that:

training data are sampled from a distribution P;
future (deployment) data are drawn from the same distribution.

In practice, this assumption is often violated.



Definition
Domain shift refers to the situation where the data distribution at deployment differs from that observed during training.
Equivalently, the deployment risk \mathcal{R}_\star differs from the training risk \mathcal{R}.



Why It Occurs
Common sources of domain shift include:

Temporal effects
Data evolve over time (e.g. footfall, financial data).
Population differences
Training and deployment populations differ (e.g. medical datasets).
Sampling bias
Training data are not representative of the true environment.




Why It Matters
Even if:

empirical risk is small, and

generalisation error is small,

the model may still perform poorly if the deployment distribution differs from the training distribution.



Extended Risk Decomposition
The deployment risk can be decomposed as:

\mathcal{R}_\star(f_n)
\leq
\underbrace{
\max_{f \in \mathcal{F}} |\mathcal{R}_\star(f) - \mathcal{R}(f)|
}_{\text{domain shift}}
+
\underbrace{
\min_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(f)
}_{\text{bias}}
+
\underbrace{
\sqrt{\frac{2}{n} \log \frac{2|\mathcal{F}|}{\delta}}
}_{\text{variance}}

You do not need to memorise this formula, but you should understand the key terms and their implications.



Interpretation

Bias reflects limitations of the model class \mathcal{F}.
Variance reflects uncertainty due to finite data.
Domain shift reflects mismatch between training and deployment environments.

Domain shift is not controlled by standard generalisation bounds.



Key Insight
Generalisation theory assumes that training and test data are drawn from the same distribution.
It does not account for domain shift.



Practical Implications

Models should be validated on data that reflect deployment conditions.
Distributional assumptions must be carefully assessed.
Domain shift is a major cause of:

degraded performance,
unreliable predictions,
ethical concerns (e.g. fairness across populations).





Key Points

Domain shift is a mismatch between training and deployment data distributions.
It is distinct from generalisation error.
Standard machine learning theory does not address it.
It is often the dominant factor in real-world model performance.

Chapter 5 - Online Supervised Learning
Chapter 5 5  Online Supervised Learning studies a different paradigm for training machine learning models, where data arrive sequentially over time rather than being available in a fixed dataset.
Unlike the standard (offline) setting, where a model is trained once and then deployed, online learning continuously updates the model as new observations are received.
This chapter introduces:

the formal definition of an online supervised learning task 5.1;
the distinction between environments with and without feedback;
the concept of cumulative loss as a performance measure over time.

The examinable content from this chapter is entirely intuitive and conceptual, rather than mathematical.


  Understand the difference between offline and online supervised learning. 



Offline (Batch) Learning
In the standard supervised learning setting:

we are given a fixed dataset

\{(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{y}_i)\}_{i=1}^n;

the model is trained once by minimising empirical risk;
after training, the model is deployed without further updates.

Key feature:
All data are available in advance.



Online Learning
In online supervised learning:

data arrive sequentially over time;
at time t, the model is trained using data

\{(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{y}_i)\}_{i=1}^{t-1};

the model is updated continuously as new data arrive.

Key feature:
The model must adapt in real time.



Key Differences



Aspect
Offline Learning
Online Learning




Data availability
Fixed dataset
Sequential / streaming


Training
One-off
Continuous updates


Objective
Minimise empirical risk
Minimise cumulative loss


Adaptation
None after training
Adapts over time


Typical use
Static datasets
Dynamic environments






When Online Learning Is Needed
Online learning is particularly useful when:

data arrive in a stream;
storing all past data is impractical;
the underlying distribution may change over time
(cf. domain shift Domain Shift).




Key Points

Offline learning assumes a fixed dataset and static environment.
Online learning updates the model sequentially.
The performance measure changes from risk to cumulative loss.
Online learning is essential in dynamic or real-time settings.






  Understand the multi-armed bandit problem Bandits and the concept of regret. 



Core Idea
A multi-armed bandit models sequential decision-making under uncertainty:

there are B possible actions (bandits / arms);
each action i has an unknown expected reward \mu_i;
at each time t, we choose an action and observe a reward.




The Challenge
We do not know the values of \mu_i in advance.
To perform well, we must:

explore: try different actions to learn their rewards;
exploit: choose the best-known action to maximise reward.

This creates the fundamental exploration–exploitation trade-off.



Objective
Let

\mu_\star = \max_{1 \leq i \leq B} \mu_i

be the best possible expected reward.
The goal is to minimise the regret:

\mu_\star - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T R_t




Interpretation of Regret

Measures how much reward we lose compared to always choosing the best arm.
If we always pick the optimal bandit, regret is 0.
In practice, regret is positive because we must explore.




Why Regret Arises

The optimal action is unknown initially.
Learning requires trying suboptimal actions.
This incurs a temporary loss in reward.




Examples of Bandit Problems

Online advertising
Selecting adverts to maximise click-through rates.
Clinical trials
Allocating treatments while learning effectiveness.




Key Insight
Bandits are a simple instance of online learning where:

decisions are made sequentially;
feedback is limited (we only observe the reward of the chosen action);
performance is measured over time via regret.




Key Points

Multi-armed bandit = sequential decision problem with unknown rewards.
Must balance exploration and exploitation.
Performance is measured using regret, not risk.
Regret quantifies the cost of learning.

Chapter 7 - Ethics of Machine Learning
Chapter 7 7  Ethics of Machine Learning considers the ethical issues that arise when machine learning models are deployed in real-world settings.
While earlier chapters focused on the mathematical and statistical foundations of machine learning, this chapter highlights that technical performance alone is not sufficient; the use of machine learning systems can have significant societal consequences.
The chapter discusses a range of ethical considerations, including:

bias and fairness in model predictions;
responsibility and accountability for decisions made by models;
privacy and consent in the use of data;
broader societal impacts, such as environmental cost and labour market effects.

An important learning outcome is to be able to identify and explain ethical issues that may arise in a given machine learning application.


  Understand issues of (bias and fairness iss-bias-and-fairness?) in machine learning. 



What is the Issue?
Machine learning models are trained on data. If the training data are:

unrepresentative, or

reflect existing societal biases,

then the trained model may produce biased or unfair predictions.



Examples

A medical model trained only on one population (e.g. a single genetic background) may perform poorly on others.
A financial model may assign different outcomes (e.g. loan rates) to similar individuals based on features correlated with protected characteristics.




Key Idea
Bias can arise because the model:

learns patterns present in the data;
cannot distinguish between correlation and fairness.




Defining Fairness
A central difficulty is that fairness is not uniquely defined.
Different notions include:

equal outcomes across groups;
equal error rates across groups;
decisions based only on “relevant” features.

These definitions can conflict with each other.



Trade-off with Performance
Improving fairness may:

require constraining the model;
reduce performance with respect to the original objective (e.g. prediction accuracy or risk 1.3).




Mitigation
Fairness can be incorporated by modifying the training objective, for example:

\mathcal{R}_n(f) + \lambda R(f),

where R(f) penalises unfair behaviour.
(See regularisation Regularisation.)



Key Points

Bias arises from data and modelling choices.
Fairness is difficult to define and measure.
Different definitions of fairness may conflict.
There is often a trade-off between fairness and performance.
Regularisation can be used to encourage fair behaviour.






  Understand issues of autonomy and responsibility in machine learning ((iss-autonomy?)). 



What is the Issue?
When a machine learning model is deployed in the real world, it may make decisions that have serious consequences (e.g. financial, legal, or physical harm).
This raises the question:

Who is responsible when something goes wrong?




Sources of Failure
Harmful outcomes may arise from:

errors in code (bugs);
poor or biased training data;
incorrect modelling assumptions;
adversarial attacks (e.g. data poisoning).

Responsibility may depend on the source of the failure.



Accountability
Possible parties include:

the model developer;
the organisation deploying the model;
regulators or oversight bodies.

In practice, responsibility is often unclear and shared.



Autonomy vs Human Oversight
Machine learning systems can operate with a high degree of autonomy.
Key questions:

Should humans remain in the loop for important decisions?
Should fully automated decision-making be allowed in high-stakes settings?




Transparency and Explainability
There is increasing demand for:

the ability to challenge decisions made by models;
explanations of how decisions were made.

However:

many models (e.g. neural networks) are difficult to interpret;
models may be protected as corporate intellectual property.




Regulation and Control
Questions arise about:

whether AI systems should be regulated;
whether outputs (e.g. political content) should be controlled;
how to balance innovation with safety and accountability.




Key Points

Machine learning systems can cause real-world harm.
Responsibility for decisions is often unclear.
Failures can arise from data, models, or external attacks.
There is a tension between autonomy and human oversight.
Transparency and regulation are central ethical challenges.






  Understand issues of (AI in warfare iss-warfare?). 



What is the Issue?
Machine learning and AI are increasingly being used in military contexts, including:

surveillance;
target identification;
autonomous or semi-autonomous weapons systems.

This raises serious ethical and legal concerns.



Legal Considerations
Military use of AI must comply with international law, including:

the Geneva Convention;
rules prohibiting attacks on civilians.

Key question:

how can we ensure that decisions made by a model are legally compliant?




Human Oversight
A central issue is whether life-and-death decisions should be:

fully automated; or

subject to human control (“human-in-the-loop”).




Risk and Failure
Machine learning systems can:

fail unpredictably;
behave incorrectly in unfamiliar situations;
be vulnerable to adversarial manipulation.

In a military setting, such failures could have catastrophic consequences.



Responsibility
As with (autonomy and responsibility iss-autonomy?):

it may be unclear who is accountable for decisions made by AI systems in warfare.




Broader Ethical Questions

Should AI be used in warfare at all?
Does increased effectiveness justify ethical risks?
What level of regulation or international agreement is needed?




Key Points

AI is increasingly used in military decision-making.
There are serious concerns about legality and civilian safety.
Human oversight is a key ethical issue.
Failures can have catastrophic consequences.
Responsibility and regulation remain open questions.






  Understand issues of (consent to data use iss-consent?). 



What is the Issue?
Machine learning models require large amounts of data, often collected from:

the internet (e.g. text, images);
personal or institutional records (e.g. health data).

This raises questions about consent and ownership of data.



Copyright and Data Use

Training data may include copyrighted material.
Data are often collected without explicit permission from creators.

Key questions:

Should creators receive compensation for use of their data?
Is training a model fundamentally different from copying content?




Personal Data and Consent
Even when data are anonymised, concerns remain:

individuals may not be aware their data are used;
anonymisation may not fully prevent re-identification.

Example:

health records used for research or commercial purposes.




Trade-offs
There is a tension between:

innovation and progress in AI;
individual rights to privacy and consent.

Relaxing restrictions may:

accelerate research and development;

but may also:

reduce protections for individuals.




Regulation
The legal framework is currently:

evolving;
often unclear.

Governments are actively considering how to regulate:

data usage;
copyright in machine learning.




Key Points

Machine learning relies on large-scale data collection.
Consent is often unclear or absent.
Copyright and ownership of training data are contested.
Anonymisation does not guarantee privacy.
There is a trade-off between innovation and individual protection.
Regulation in this area is still developing.






  Understand issues of (environmental impact iss-environmental-impact?). 



What is the Issue?
Training large machine learning models can require substantial computational resources, leading to:

high electricity usage;
significant carbon emissions;
additional resource costs (e.g. cooling, water).




Scale of the Problem
Modern models (e.g. large language models) can require:

massive datasets;
large-scale parallel computation (e.g. GPUs running for weeks).

This leads to very high energy consumption.



Trade-offs
There is a tension between:

environmental cost, and

societal benefit (e.g. improved technology, productivity).

Key questions:

Are these energy costs justified?
Should there be limits on large-scale model training?




Broader Impacts

Growth in data centres increases overall energy demand.
Environmental impact may increase if many organisations compete to train large models.




Regulation and Policy
Possible responses include:

improving energy efficiency;
using renewable energy sources;
regulating large-scale compute usage.




Key Points

Machine learning can have a significant environmental footprint.
Training large models requires substantial energy.
There is a trade-off between innovation and sustainability.
The cumulative impact of widespread model training is a concern.
Policy and regulation may play an important role.






  Understand issues of (job displacement and labour market impact iss-job-impact?). 



What is the Issue?
Machine learning and AI have the potential to transform the labour market, including:

automating existing jobs;
creating new types of work;
changing required skill sets.




Job Displacement
Some roles may be at risk, particularly:

repetitive or routine tasks;
roles in manufacturing, logistics, and customer service.




Uncertainty
The overall impact is difficult to predict:

past technological advances have both destroyed and created jobs;
new capabilities (e.g. generative models) can disrupt unexpected sectors.




Job Creation
AI may also create:

roles in development, maintenance, and deployment;
new industries and services.




Transition Challenges
Key concerns include:

speed of change;
ability of workers to retrain or adapt;
potential short-term increases in unemployment or inequality.




Key Questions

Which sectors will be most affected?
Will the overall impact be positive or negative?
How will this affect future career paths?




Key Points

AI can both displace and create jobs.
The net effect is uncertain and context-dependent.
Rapid change may create social and economic challenges.
Adaptation and reskilling are important considerations.






  Understand issues of (inequality iss-inequality?). 



What is the Issue?
Machine learning and AI may affect different groups unequally, potentially:

benefiting some individuals or regions more than others;
widening existing social or economic inequalities.




Potential Risks

Wealthy organisations and nations may have greater access to:

data;
computational resources;
expertise.

This may lead to concentration of power and wealth.




Democratising Potential
On the other hand, AI tools (e.g. chatbots) may:

provide widespread access to knowledge;
lower barriers to education and productivity.

This could have a democratising effect.



Key Tension

Inequality may increase due to uneven access to resources;
vs

Inequality may decrease due to wider access to powerful tools.




Key Points

AI may either exacerbate or reduce inequality.
Outcomes depend on access to technology and resources.
Distribution of benefits is a central concern.
The long-term impact is uncertain.






  Understand issues of (human interaction iss-human-interaction?). 



What is the Issue?
AI is increasingly integrated into everyday life, influencing how people:

interact with technology;
communicate with each other;
form relationships.




Societal Impact
AI systems (e.g. virtual assistants, chatbots) may:

change patterns of communication;
reduce or replace certain forms of human interaction;
influence behaviour and decision-making.




Human–AI Relationships
There is evidence that people may:

form emotional or personal connections with AI systems;
rely on AI for companionship or advice.

This raises concerns about:

dependency;
manipulation;
psychological effects.




Vulnerable Groups
Concerns may be greater for:

children;
individuals more susceptible to influence.

This raises questions about appropriate safeguards and regulation.



Key Questions

How should AI systems interact with users?
Should there be limits on AI influence?
Should children’s interaction with AI be regulated?




Key Points

AI is changing human interaction patterns.
Human–AI relationships raise new ethical concerns.
Vulnerable users may require additional protections.
The societal impact is still evolving.






  Understand issues of (veracity and trust iss-trust?). 



What is the Issue?
Advances in AI (e.g. text-to-image, text-to-video) make it possible to generate highly realistic synthetic content.
This creates challenges for trust and authenticity.



Risks

AI-generated content may be:

misleading;
difficult to distinguish from real data;
used for misinformation or manipulation.

This can undermine trust in:

media;
institutions;
digital information.





Lack of Safeguards
Currently:

there is no universal system for verifying authenticity;
regulation is limited or evolving.




Key Questions

How can we detect AI-generated content?
Should content be labelled or regulated?
What responsibilities do creators and platforms have?




Broader Impact

Reduced trust in information may affect:

education;
politics;
public discourse.





Key Points

AI enables realistic synthetic content generation.
This creates challenges for trust and authenticity.
Misinformation risks are significant.
Regulation and detection methods are still developing.
